summary:
Scotland is a constituent nation of the United Kingdom. Criminal law, policing, prisons and family law are devolved to the Scottish Parliament, while legal gender recognition and equality law are set at United Kingdom level; the findings set out here are those specific to Scotland.

Hate crime in Scotland is governed by the Hate Crime and Public Order (Scotland) Act 2021, passed by the Scottish Parliament in March 2021 by 82 votes to 32, given royal assent a month later and brought into force on 1 April 2024. It lists gender identity as a protected characteristic. Earlier Scottish legislation from 2009 provides for penalty enhancements where an offence is motivated by the victim's gender identity, alongside sexual orientation.

The Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service recorded 7,115 hate-crime charges in 2025-26, 17 per cent more than in 2024-25 and the highest total since 2003-04. Charges with a sexual-orientation aggravation numbered 2,062, the second most common category. Charges with a transgender-identity aggravation numbered 104, up 21 per cent from 86 and the highest figure since the 2021 Act took effect. Transgender-identity aggravations remain a small share of the total, and the increase is measured in raw counts.

Police-recorded hate crime for 2024-25, the first annual report under the 2021 Act, totalled 8,538 offences. Race was the aggravator in 62 per cent of them and sexual orientation in just over a quarter. The highest rates per 10,000 residents were in Glasgow City and the City of Edinburgh, at about 32.25 each.

Reform of gender recognition in Scotland has not taken effect. The Scottish Government announced in 2018 that it would add an "X" sex descriptor to identity documents and lower the minimum age of transition to 16. A Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill, applying only to Scotland, was introduced in March 2022 and passed by the Scottish Parliament in December 2022 by 86 votes to 39. The United Kingdom government blocked it under section 35 of the Scotland Act 1998, the first use of that power to overturn Scottish legislation, and it did not receive royal assent.

Same-sex marriage has been lawful in Scotland since 16 December 2014 under the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Scotland) Act 2014, passed on 4 February 2014 by 108 votes to 15, with royal assent on 12 March 2014 and first ceremonies on 31 December 2014. No religious organisation or celebrant is obliged to solemnise such a marriage. Civil partnerships have been available since 2005 under the Civil Partnership Act 2004.
tangentialFactors:
The United Kingdom government's use of section 35 of the Scotland Act 1998 to block the Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill was the first exercise of that power against Scottish legislation. A reform passed by 86 votes to 39 in the Scottish Parliament therefore did not reach the statute book, and gender recognition in Scotland continues to run through the United Kingdom process.

Recorded hate crime is concentrated in Glasgow City and the City of Edinburgh on a per-capita basis, at about 32.25 per 10,000 residents each. That measure reflects where people live and report offences as much as where offences occur.

Transgender-identity aggravations form a small part of the total hate-crime picture in Scotland: 104 of 7,115 charges in 2025-26, against 2,062 sexual-orientation aggravations and a race aggravator in 62 per cent of police-recorded offences. The 21 per cent rise on that base is a change of 18 charges.

The Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service figure of 7,115 charges for 2025-26 and the police-recorded figure of 8,538 offences for 2024-25 are different measures for different periods and do not indicate a fall in recorded hate crime.
localsOnly:
Civil partnerships in Scotland, available since 2005 under the Civil Partnership Act 2004, confer property, inheritance tax, social security, pension, parental responsibility, maintenance, tenancy, insurance and next-of-kin rights, with formal dissolution on terms akin to divorce.

Same-sex couples have held joint and stepchild adoption rights in Scotland since 28 September 2009, and the Looked After Children (Scotland) Regulations 2009 allow them to be considered as foster parents on the same basis as anyone else.
outOfScopeNotes:
No per-capita rate for transgender-identity aggravated charges is sourced, so the 104 charges recorded in 2025-26 cannot be compared with the general hate-crime rate; the 21 per cent rise is a change on a small base.

Prosecution and conviction outcomes for transgender-identity aggravators are not sourced, and it is unresolved whether the 2021 Act's gender-identity provisions are applied consistently across Police Scotland divisions.

The two hate-crime datasets cited here use different measures and cover different years, and the sources do not reconcile them.

The practical effect of the blocked Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill on current administrative practice in Scotland is unresolved. The interaction between Scotland's marriage law and the United Kingdom process for issuing gender recognition certificates, including the requirement that a spouse consent, is not addressed by the Scotland-specific sources here.

No Scotland-specific data on violence against transgender people beyond recorded hate-crime aggravators is sourced.
